title: Parts of Speech
subtitle: The Eight Clans of Wordland
intro: In Wordland, every word belongs to a clan, and each clan has one job. Learn the eight clans and every sentence becomes a team you can read at a glance.

rules.title: Nouns
rules.tagline: The Name Clan: people, places, things and ideas

story.line: Hana arrives at the gates of the Grammar Shrine. A giant owl blocks the path.
Halt, traveler! Before you enter, you must give me your name.
I'm Hana! I came from the village to learn every rule of English.
Then you have already used the first clan. Hana, village, rule: each one names something. They are nouns.
Hmph. So a noun is just a person?
A person, a place, a thing, or even an idea you cannot touch, like courage or friendship.

parts.name: Common nouns
parts.detail: General names for any member of a group. They start with a lowercase letter.

parts.name: Proper nouns
parts.detail: The special name of one particular person, place or thing. Always capitalized.

parts.name: Concrete vs. abstract
parts.detail: Concrete nouns can be sensed (sword, rain). Abstract nouns are ideas or feelings (courage, time).
parts.example: Her courage was stronger than the storm.

parts.name: Collective nouns
parts.detail: One word for a group: team, family, flock, class.

rules.history:
The word noun comes from Latin nomen, which simply means name.

About 2,100 years ago, a Greek scholar named Dionysius Thrax wrote a short grammar book that sorted Greek words into eight parts of speech. Roman teachers copied his list for Latin, and English schoolbooks copied the Romans. That is why English still talks about eight word clans today, and why nouns are always the first one you meet.

examples.note: Tokyo is a proper noun, so it is capitalized. City is common, so it is not.
Friendship and strength are abstract nouns: you can't touch them, but they are still things.

examples.good: A flock of birds circled the shrine.
examples.note: Flock is a collective noun for many birds.

rules.trick: If you can put 'a', 'the' or 'my' in front of it, it is probably a noun: a sword, the shrine, my courage.

quiz.q: Which word is a noun? 'The brave girl smiled.'

quiz.why: Japan is the special name of one place, so it is proper and capitalized.

rules.title: Pronouns
rules.tagline: The Shadow Clan that stands in for nouns

story.line: Kaito drew Kaito's sword, and Kaito swung Kaito's sword at Kaito's enemy!
Ehehe, you said your own name four times. Are you trying to summon yourself?
Call the Shadow Clan. They take a noun's place so you don't repeat it.
Fine. Kaito drew his sword, and he swung it at his enemy.
He, his, it: they are like shadows that follow the noun around!

parts.name: Personal
parts.detail: I, you, he, she, it, we, they (and me, him, her, us, them).

parts.name: Possessive
parts.detail: Show ownership: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. No apostrophes!

parts.name: Reflexive
parts.detail: Point back to the subject: myself, yourself, himself, themselves.

parts.name: Demonstrative & relative
parts.detail: Point or connect: this, that, these, those, who, which, that.
parts.example: This is the sword that never breaks.

parts.name: Antecedent
parts.detail: The noun a pronoun replaces. The pronoun must match it in number.

rules.history:
Pronoun comes from Latin pro nomine, meaning 'for a name' or 'in place of a noun.'

Old English had many more pronoun forms because every word changed its ending depending on its job. Most of those forms disappeared, but pronouns kept theirs. That is why we still say he, him, his, while nouns like sword barely change at all. Pronouns are the last survivors of the old case system.

examples.good: Hana lost her map, so she asked for help.
examples.bad: Hana lost Hana's map, so Hana asked for help.
examples.note: Her and she replace Hana.
Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes.

examples.good: Each student brought their own lunch.
examples.note: Singular they has been used in English for over 600 years.

rules.trick: Pronouns are shadows: they can't exist without the noun they follow. If a reader can't tell who 'he' is, the shadow has lost its owner.

quiz.q: Choose the correct possessive: 'The dragon guarded ___ treasure.'
Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
quiz.why: Reflexive pronouns point back to the subject: she ... herself.

rules.title: Verbs
rules.tagline: The Action Clan: the heartbeat of every sentence

story.line: In the training yard, Kaito stands frozen like a statue.
Kaito, why aren't you moving?
Someone wrote my sentence as 'Kaito the sword.' There's no action word, so I can't do anything!
Without a verb, a sentence has no heartbeat. Give him one, Hana.
Kaito swings the sword!
I'm free! Hyaaah!
Remember: some verbs are quiet. 'Kaito is tired' has a verb too. Is shows a state of being.

parts.name: Action verbs
parts.detail: Show something being done: run, fight, think, write.
parts.example: The dragon flies over the city.

parts.name: Linking verbs
parts.detail: Connect the subject to a description: be, seem, become, feel, look.

parts.name: Helping verbs
parts.detail: Team up with a main verb to show time or mood: be, have, do, will, can, must.

parts.name: Tense
parts.detail: Verbs change form to show when something happens: walk, walked, will walk.
parts.example: Yesterday he walked; today he walks.

rules.history:
Verb comes from Latin verbum, which means simply 'word.' The Romans thought the verb was so important that it was THE word of a sentence.

English verbs used to have many more endings. In Shakespeare's time people said 'he walketh' and 'thou walkest.' Over the 1500s and 1600s the -s ending, which had spread down from northern England, replaced -eth, leaving us with 'he walks.'

examples.note: Laughs is an action verb.
Seems is a linking verb: it describes the shrine, not an action.
Helping verb will comes before the main verb win.

rules.trick: Try putting 'I', 'you' or 'they' in front of the word. If it makes sense (I run, they think), it can be a verb.

quiz.q: Find the verb: 'The ninja vanished into the mist.'
In 'Hana feels happy,' what kind of verb is 'feels'?
quiz.why: It links Hana to the description happy.

rules.title: Adjectives
rules.tagline: The Color Clan that describes nouns

story.line: A mysterious scroll appears. It reads: 'Beware the dragon.'
A dragon? I'll fight it! ...Wait, what kind of dragon?
Hehe. A tiny, sleepy, pink dragon. Or maybe a huge, angry, ancient one.
Those describing words change everything!
They are adjectives. They paint color onto nouns and tell you which one, what kind, or how many.

parts.name: Describing
parts.detail: What kind? red, ancient, brave, sleepy.

parts.name: Quantity
parts.detail: How many or how much? three, several, many, few.

parts.name: Position
parts.detail: Usually before the noun, or after a linking verb.
parts.example: the brave hero / The hero is brave.

parts.name: Comparison
parts.detail: Adjectives can compare: tall, taller, tallest.

rules.history:
Adjective comes from Latin adiectivum, meaning 'something added.' Roman grammarians saw these words as extras thrown onto a noun.

In Old English, adjectives changed their endings to match the noun they described, just like in German today. After the Norman Conquest in 1066, those endings wore away. Modern English adjectives never change for number: one red lantern, two red lanterns.

examples.note: English adjectives never take a plural -s.
Cold follows the linking verb was and still describes night.
Two adjectives describe one noun.

rules.trick: Adjectives answer the three questions of a curious kitsune: Which one? What kind? How many?

quiz.q: Which word is an adjective? 'The fierce tiger slept.'

quiz.why: Adjectives stay the same even when the noun is plural.

rules.title: Adverbs
rules.tagline: The Wind Clan that describes how, when and where

story.line: I attacked!
How? When? Where? Your story is a blank wall, Kaito.
Uh... I attacked quickly. Yesterday. Outside.
Quickly, yesterday, outside! They describe the verb, like wind giving it speed and direction.
Adverbs can even describe adjectives and other adverbs: very fast, extremely quickly.

parts.name: How (manner)
parts.detail: Often end in -ly: quickly, quietly, bravely.

parts.name: When (time)
parts.detail: now, later, yesterday, soon, already.

parts.name: Where (place)
parts.detail: here, there, outside, everywhere.

parts.name: How much (degree)
parts.detail: very, too, almost, extremely. They power up adjectives and adverbs.

parts.name: How often (frequency)
parts.detail: always, usually, sometimes, never.

rules.history:
The -ly ending comes from the Old English word lic, which meant 'body' or 'form.' So 'bravely' once meant something like 'in a brave form.'

The same word lic also became the modern word like. That is why 'friendly' and 'friend-like' feel so similar. They are twins separated at birth!

examples.note: Quickly describes how she runs. Quick is the adjective form.
Very boosts the adjective large.
Frequency adverbs usually sit before the main verb.

rules.trick: Ask the verb three wind questions: How? When? Where? Whatever answers is an adverb.

quiz.q: Which word is an adverb? 'The ninja moved silently.'
quiz.why: Silently tells how the ninja moved.
Use the adverb beautifully to describe the verb sings.

rules.title: Prepositions
rules.tagline: The Map Clan that shows position and connection

story.line: Hana searches for the hidden key.
The key is... somewhere. Fufufu.
That's useless! Is it in the box? Under the box? Behind the box?
You have discovered the Map Clan. In, under, behind: prepositions show where things are and how they connect.
Fine, fine. It's under the cushion, beside the lantern, in the tea room.

parts.name: Place
parts.detail: in, on, under, between, behind, above.
parts.example: The cat is under the table.

parts.name: Time
parts.detail: at, on, in, before, after, during, since.

parts.name: Direction
parts.detail: to, into, toward, through, across.

parts.name: Prepositional phrase
parts.detail: A preposition plus its object (a noun or pronoun).

rules.history:
Preposition comes from Latin praepositio, meaning 'placed before,' because it sits before its noun.

Old English used word endings to show many relationships, like 'to the king' being shown just by changing the ending of 'king.' As those endings disappeared after 1066, English leaned more and more on little words like to, of and with to do that job. That's why modern English has so many prepositions.

examples.good: The scroll is on the shelf.
examples.note: On shows position.
During shows time.

examples.good: Between you and me, Yumi lies a lot.
examples.bad: Between you and I, Yumi lies a lot.
examples.note: After a preposition, use object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them.

rules.trick: Think of a box and a cat. Anything the cat can do to the box (in, on, under, beside, around) is a preposition.

quiz.q: Find the preposition: 'The ninja hid behind the wall.'
quiz.why: Behind shows where the ninja hid.

quiz.q: Choose the correct one: 'This is between you and ___.'
quiz.why: Prepositions take object pronouns, so 'between you and me.'

rules.title: Conjunctions
rules.tagline: The Bridge Clan that joins words and ideas

story.line: I'm hungry. I'm tired. I want ramen. The shop is closed.
You sound like a robot.
Use the Bridge Clan. Join your thoughts.
I'm hungry and tired, so I want ramen, but the shop is closed because it's midnight.
Ooh, and, so, but, because. Now it sounds like a sad anime episode.

parts.name: Coordinating (FANBOYS)
parts.detail: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. They join equal parts.
parts.example: I like tea, but she likes coffee.

parts.name: Subordinating
parts.detail: Begin a dependent idea: because, although, when, if, since, unless.
parts.example: We stayed inside because it rained.

parts.name: Correlative pairs
parts.detail: Work in pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also.
parts.example: Either we fight, or we run.

rules.history:
Conjunction comes from Latin coniungere, 'to join together.' The same root gives us the word junction, where roads meet.

Many old grammar books once taught that you must never start a sentence with and or but. That was a classroom habit, not a real rule. Writers from the Old English era to the King James Bible to modern novels have started sentences with And and But.

examples.good: I wanted to go, but I was sick.
examples.note: Use a comma before a FANBOYS word joining two full sentences.

examples.good: Although it was late, we kept training.
examples.note: Although starts a dependent clause.

examples.good: Neither Kaito nor Yumi finished the homework.
examples.bad: Neither Kaito or Yumi finished the homework.
examples.note: Neither pairs with nor.

rules.trick: Remember the FANBOYS: For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. They are the seven bridges of the kingdom.

quiz.why: Yet is one of the FANBOYS.

rules.title: Interjections
rules.tagline: The Spirit Clan of sudden feelings

story.line: A giant spider drops from the ceiling.
Aaah! Yikes!
Wow. Brave warrior, huh?
Oops, I think that was just Sensei's toy.
Aah, yikes, wow, oops: interjections burst out with feelings. They stand alone and need no grammar friends.

parts.name: Strong feelings
parts.detail: Usually followed by an exclamation mark.

parts.name: Mild feelings
parts.detail: Can be followed by a comma.
parts.example: Oh, I didn't see you there.

parts.name: Greetings and responses
parts.detail: Hello, yes, no, thanks, hey.

rules.history:
Interjection comes from Latin interiectio, meaning 'something thrown in between.' Ancient grammarians noticed these words get tossed into speech without connecting to the rest of the sentence.

Interjections change fast with fashion. Shakespeare's characters cry 'Alas!' and 'Fie!', while today we might say 'Oops' or 'Yikes.'

examples.note: Strong feeling, exclamation mark.
Mild feeling, comma.

examples.good: Oh no, I forgot my sword.
examples.note: Interjections often start a sentence.

rules.trick: If you could shout it in an anime reaction shot, it's an interjection.

quiz.q: Best punctuation: 'Ouch ___ I stepped on a tack.'
quiz.why: A strong feeling gets an exclamation mark.
